steps.body: sin x fails the horizontal line test spectacularly — every output is hit infinitely often — so, recall the rescue: **restrict the domain**. Keep only **[−π/2, π/2]**, one clean climb from −1 to 1. THAT piece is one-to-one, and its inverse is **arcsin** (also written sin⁻¹).

predict.prompt: sin 150° = 1/2 too. Can the drag reach 150° to claim it as arcsin(1/2)?

options.label: No — the branch stops at 90°; only one angle per sine value is allowed in
Yes — any angle with the right sine counts
Yes, by dragging the long way around

predict.reveal: No — you hit a wall at 90°. That wall is the whole point: inside [−90°, 90°] every sine value appears exactly once, so “the angle whose sine is 1/2” picks out one answer. Feel for the wall, then land on 30°.

widget.prompt: Only the arc from −90° to 90° is open — the rest is walled off. Find the one angle in this branch whose sine is 1/2.
widget.successFeedback: 30° — π/6, the n = 6 above. Inside the branch, sine climbs steadily from −1 to 1 and never repeats a value, so arcsin can answer with a single angle. The wall you bumped at 90° is what makes the inverse a function.
widget.lowFeedback: The sine here is below 1/2 — climb counterclockwise and watch the sin readout rise toward 0.5.
widget.highFeedback: The sine here is above 1/2 — ease back down. (And if you were hunting 150°: the wall already told you that door is closed.)

explanationVariants: 5π/6 also has sine 1/2, but it sits OUTSIDE the restricted branch [−π/2, π/2] — the restriction is exactly what makes arcsin single-valued.
A function returns one output; the domain restriction chose which of the infinitely many candidate angles survives: π/6.

options.label: 5π/6 is outside the restricted branch [−π/2, π/2] that defines arcsin
options.feedback: Right — the restriction discarded it, the same move that defined √x from x² (recall).

options.label: Because 5π/6 is negative
options.feedback: 5π/6 ≈ 2.6 is positive — the issue is it exceeds π/2, leaving the kept branch.

options.label: It is — arcsin has two values
options.feedback: A FUNCTION can't return two values. The restriction picks exactly one: π/6.

explanationVariants: arcsin(−1/2) = −π/6: the branch includes negative angles, and sin(−π/6) = −1/2.
The kept climb passes through negatives — no reference-angle gymnastics needed: just −π/6.

options.label: −π/6
options.feedback: Right — the branch [−π/2, π/2] handles negatives directly: sin(−π/6) = −1/2.

options.label: 5π/6
options.feedback: sin(5π/6) = +1/2, wrong sign — and 5π/6 isn't in the branch anyway. Answer: −π/6.

options.label: 7π/6
options.feedback: sin(7π/6) = −1/2 is true, but 7π/6 lies far outside [−π/2, π/2]. The branch's angle is −π/6.

steps.body: Domain and range swap (recall): sin on the branch has domain [−π/2, π/2] and range [−1, 1], so **arcsin has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2]**. Inputs beyond ±1 are meaningless — no angle has sine 2.

explanationVariants: arcsin(2) asks for an angle whose sine is 2 — impossible, since sine never leaves [−1, 1]: undefined.
arcsin's domain is sin's RANGE: [−1, 1]. 2 is outside.

options.label: Undefined — no angle has sine 2
options.feedback: Right — sine's outputs fill only [−1, 1], so arcsin accepts only [−1, 1].

options.label: π/2
options.feedback: arcsin(1) = π/2 — sine's MAXIMUM is 1, so 2 is unreachable: undefined.

options.label: About 1.09
options.feedback: That's arcsin of ≈0.89. For the input 2 there is no angle at all: undefined.

explanationVariants: arcsin(1) = π/2: the branch's right endpoint, where the climb tops out at sine 1. n = 2.
The only angle in [−π/2, π/2] with sine 1 is π/2 itself.
hints: Which angle in the branch has sine exactly 1?
Sine reaches 1 at the top of the unit circle.

commonErrors.feedback: sin π = 0, not 1. Sine hits 1 at π/2: n = 2.
π/6 has sine 1/2. The FULL value 1 needs π/2: n = 2.

takeaways: arcsin inverts sine's restricted climb on [−π/2, π/2].
Domain [−1, 1], range [−π/2, π/2]; negatives handled directly.
Candidate angles outside the branch are discarded by definition.
steps.teaser: Next: cosine needs a DIFFERENT branch — and tangent gets one with asymptotes.

concept.body: arcsin(v) = the unique angle in [−π/2, π/2] whose sine is v. Check any answer two ways: sine of it gives v, AND it lies in the branch.

explanationVariants: sin 0 = 0 and 0 is in the branch: arcsin(0) = 0.
The climb crosses height 0 exactly at its center, angle 0.

commonErrors.feedback: sin π = 0 too, but π is outside [−π/2, π/2]. The branch's angle is 0.
arcsin returns an ANGLE; the angle with sine 0 in the branch is 0 itself.
